recommendations.title: Add a MongoDB healthcheck and an autoheal sidecar to the compose stack
recommendations.rationale: In experiment b83163af6f18 (risk LOW 1.5/10), API success fell to 89% during injection, TTR 47 s. Docker's `restart: always` only reacts to a process exit; a container that is running but marked `unhealthy` is never restarted. Without a healthcheck on mongodb nothing even notices a wedged database, and dependents that lost their connection just sit there.
steps: Add to the mongodb service: `healthcheck: {test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"], interval: 10s, timeout: 5s, retries: 3, start_period: 20s}`.
Add an `autoheal` service: `image: willfarrell/autoheal`, `environment: [AUTOHEAL_CONTAINER_LABEL=all]`, mount `/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro`, `restart: always`.
Label the Ditto services with `autoheal=true` (or keep `AUTOHEAL_CONTAINER_LABEL=all`) so an `unhealthy` state triggers a restart.
verify: `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' mongodb` reports `healthy` at steady state.
Pause mongodb for 60 s: autoheal logs show a restart of the unhealthy dependents within ~30 s of them flipping to unhealthy.

recommendations.title: Protect the data volume: log rotation, dedicated Mongo volume, free-space alerts
recommendations.rationale: In experiment b83163af6f18 (risk LOW 1.5/10), API success fell to 89% during injection, TTR 47 s. A full disk takes MongoDB (and therefore all of Ditto) down and can corrupt the WiredTiger journal; on a single host the most common culprit is unbounded container logs sharing the same filesystem.
steps: Add `logging: {driver: json-file, options: {max-size: "50m", max-file: "5"}}` to every service (or set it in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`).
Put `/data/db` on a dedicated named volume or block device separate from the Docker root and container logs.
Set `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB` explicitly (≈50% of the container memory limit) so mongod does not assume host RAM.
Alert on `node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 0.15` for the Mongo volume and on `mongodb_ss_wt_cache_bytes_currently_in_the_cache` nearing the cache size.
verify: `docker inspect mongodb --format '{{json .HostConfig.LogConfig}}'` shows the size cap; `df -h` on the Mongo volume shows > 20% free after a 24 h soak.
Replay `disk_pressure` against the app container: MongoDB keeps serving because its volume is unaffected.

recommendations.title: Baseline observability: SLO alert rules and chaos annotations in Grafana
recommendations.rationale: In experiment b83163af6f18 (risk LOW 1.5/10), API success fell to 89% during injection, TTR 47 s. Whatever the specific fault, the first production improvement is knowing within a minute that users are affected. Alert on what the user sees (probe success, error rate, p95), not only on container liveness.
steps: Prometheus rules: `probe_success == 0 for 1m` (blackbox on `/api/2/things` through nginx), API error-rate SLO burn (`sum(rate(requests{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests[5m])) > 0.02`), and `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) > 1s for 5m`.
Add a Grafana annotation (HTTP API `POST /api/annotations`, tag `chaos`) at the start and end of each Faultline experiment so latency spikes are attributable.
Dashboard the Docker health state per container (`container_health_status` via cAdvisor or a tiny exporter) next to the API SLIs.
verify: During the next experiment an alert fires within 60 s of the first API error and the Grafana graph shows the chaos window.

recommendations.title: Tune MongoDB write concern and journaling to mitigate latency under disk pressure
recommendations.rationale: [LLM suggestion, unverified] During disk pressure MongoDB slows writes, causing Ditto API latency spikes. Adjusting write concern and journaling reduces the amount of data flushed per operation, keeping response times acceptable while still preserving durability guarantees appropriate for the service.
steps: Edit the mongo-compose service in docker‑compose.yml to add environment variables: MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME, MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD (if not already set) and set the command flag '--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB=1' to limit cache pressure.

Create an init script (e.g., /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-tune.sh) that runs 'mongo --eval "db.adminCommand({setParameter:1, journalCommitIntervalMs:500})"' to increase journal commit interval, and 'db.getMongo().writeConcern = { w: 1, j: false }' to relax write acknowledgment.
Restart the stack and verify that the MongoDB container starts with the new parameters.
verify: Run a short write‑heavy load (e.g., using mongostat) and confirm write latency stays below 200 ms under normal disk usage.
Re‑run the chaos experiment (disk fill) and check that Ditto API p95 stays < 3 s and success rate remains > 95 %.

recommendations.title: Add a circuit‑breaker and fallback cache in Ditto gateway for MongoDB latency spikes
recommendations.rationale: [LLM suggestion, unverified] When MongoDB becomes slow, Ditto services continue to forward requests, amplifying latency and eventually triggering the safety abort. A circuit‑breaker that opens on high MongoDB latency and serves stale data from an in‑memory cache prevents cascading failures and keeps the API available.
steps: Introduce a resilience library (e.g., resilience4j) into the Ditto gateway codebase.
Wrap all MongoDB client calls with a TimeLimiter (e.g., 2 s) and a CircuitBreaker that opens after 5 consecutive timeouts.
When the circuit is open, read from a read‑through cache (e.g., Caffeine) populated on successful reads; writes can be queued or rejected with a clear error code.
Add metrics (breaker state, cache hit‑rate) to the Ditto metrics exporter.
Deploy the updated gateway image via the compose file (replace the image tag).
verify: Inject artificial latency (e.g., using `tc` or the existing disk‑pressure chaos) and confirm that the circuit opens after the configured threshold.
During the open state, verify that API latency drops back to baseline (< 500 ms) and that the success rate stays > 95 %.
Check Prometheus metrics for circuit‑breaker state transitions and cache hit‑rate.

recommendations.title: Tune Ditto's MongoDB client timeouts and connection pool
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7ec64f7a1498 (risk LOW 2.3/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 121 s. With default driver settings a stalled Mongo socket can hold a request thread for tens of seconds, which inflates p95 and keeps the health endpoints green while users see timeouts. Explicit, short timeouts turn a hang into a fast, retryable error.
steps: Set connection/read timeouts on the Ditto services; Ditto reads `MONGO_DB_*` environment variables (e.g. `MONGO_DB_CONNECTION_POOL_SIZE`, `MONGO_DB_READ_PREFERENCE`, `MONGO_DB_QUERY_TIMEOUT`) — verify exact names against `ditto-mongo.conf` in the Ditto source and the operating docs before applying.
Alternatively encode them in the URI: `?connectTimeoutMS=3000&socketTimeoutMS=10000&serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000&maxPoolSize=100`.
Keep `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` well below the nginx `proxy_read_timeout` so the edge sees a clean 5xx instead of a hung connection.
verify: During a `network_delay` experiment on mongodb the p95 should plateau near the configured timeout instead of growing unbounded.
`docker logs things | grep -i 'MongoTimeout'` shows fast failures rather than minute-long waits.

recommendations.title: Right-size container resources and rate-limit the edge
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7ec64f7a1498 (risk LOW 2.3/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 121 s. In our baseline the Java services already sit at ~80% of their 512 MB limit at idle, so any CPU or query pressure quickly turns into GC thrash and timeouts. Memory headroom, CPU limits and an edge rate limit keep one noisy tenant from degrading the whole API.
steps: Raise `mem_limit` for policies/things/things-search/gateway to ≥ 1 GB and set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70` in `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` so the heap fits under the cgroup limit.
Set `cpus:` limits (and `deploy.resources.reservations`) so one service cannot starve the others on the same host.
nginx: `limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=50r/s;` plus `limit_req zone=api burst=100 nodelay;` on `/api/`.

MongoDB: review indexes for the things/policies/search collections (`db.collection.getIndexes()`, `explain()` on slow queries from `db.setProfilingLevel(1, 100)`) and cap the Ditto driver `maxPoolSize` so a flood queues at the client instead of exhausting mongod.
verify: `docker stats` shows < 60% memory utilisation at idle and no OOMKilled events in `docker inspect`.
Replay `cpu_stress`: p95 stays below the abort threshold and nginx returns 429s for the excess rather than 5xx for everyone.

recommendations.title: Run MongoDB as a replica set so the Ditto driver can fail over
recommendations.rationale: In experiment c866d45ca5dc (risk LOW 0.7/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 22 s. MongoDB is the sole datastore for policies, things, things-search and connectivity. A single standalone mongod turns any Mongo hiccup into a full-platform outage; a replica set lets the Java driver elect a new primary and keep serving within seconds.
steps: Start mongod with `--replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all` (compose `command:`) and run `rs.initiate()` once via an init container or `docker exec`.
Add two more members (or one member plus an arbiter for the lab) on separate volumes.
Point the Ditto services at the set: `MONGO_DB_URI=mongodb://mongodb-0:27017,mongodb-1:27017,mongodb-2:27017/ditto?replicaSet=rs0&w=majority`.
Set `retryWrites=true&retryReads=true` on the URI so transient primary step-downs are retried by the driver.
verify: `docker exec mongodb mongosh --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.stateStr)'` shows one PRIMARY and ≥1 SECONDARY.
Re-run the same chaos experiment against the primary only; API success rate during injection should stay above the abort threshold and TTR should drop below 15 s.

recommendations.title: Set explicit timeouts end to end and add a circuit breaker at the API edge
recommendations.rationale: In experiment c866d45ca5dc (risk LOW 0.7/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 22 s. Latency injected into one hop propagated to the user as long hangs instead of fast failures. Without aligned timeouts each layer waits for the slowest one beneath it, request threads pile up, and the whole API degrades rather than the one slow path.
steps: nginx: `proxy_connect_timeout 2s; proxy_send_timeout 10s; proxy_read_timeout 30s;` and `proxy_next_upstream timeout`.

Ditto gateway: lower the request timeout (`ditto.gateway.http.request-timeout` / `GATEWAY_HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, default 60 s) to ~15 s; have clients send the `timeout` query parameter on commands (e.g. `?timeout=10s`) so Ditto fails fast instead of hanging.
Add a circuit breaker in front of the gateway (nginx `max_fails`/`fail_timeout`, or Envoy outlier detection) so a degraded backend sheds load for a few seconds instead of queuing.
Align Mongo driver `socketTimeoutMS` below the gateway timeout so the failure surfaces as a clean error with a cause.
verify: Replay `network_delay` with the same latency: p95 is capped near the smallest configured timeout and the error budget burn is measurable rather than a hang.
No request in the probe log exceeds the nginx `proxy_read_timeout`.

recommendations.title: Introduce an Envoy sidecar proxy for MongoDB with retry and timeout policies
recommendations.rationale: [LLM suggestion, unverified] A dedicated proxy can transparently retry failed MongoDB requests and enforce per‑request timeouts, reducing latency spikes seen during packet loss without changing application code.
steps: Add an Envoy container to the docker‑compose file, sharing the same network as the Ditto services and MongoDB
Configure Envoy listeners for the MongoDB port with a cluster pointing to the MongoDB service
Define retry policy (e.g., 3 attempts, 100ms per‑try timeout) and circuit‑breaker thresholds in the Envoy config
Update Ditto services to connect to the Envoy sidecar endpoint instead of MongoDB directly
Reload the compose stack and verify connectivity
verify: Inject the same network loss chaos and confirm p95 latency stays below 500 ms
Check Envoy stats for retry counts and timeout occurrences
Ensure no request errors surface to the API layer

recommendations.title: Set Docker‑Compose restart policy and resource limits for the MongoDB container
recommendations.rationale: [LLM suggestion, unverified] Automatic container restart on failure combined with proper CPU/memory limits prevents prolonged outages caused by transient network glitches or resource exhaustion.
steps: Edit docker‑compose.yml to add `restart: unless-stopped` (or `on-failure:5`) under the MongoDB service
Define `mem_limit` and `cpus` to give MongoDB sufficient headroom (e.g., 2GB memory, 1 CPU)
Optionally add `healthcheck` that pings MongoDB and ties into Docker’s restart logic
Deploy the updated stack
verify: During a network loss experiment, confirm the MongoDB container restarts within a few seconds if it becomes unhealthy
Observe that the container stays within the defined resource limits via `docker stats`
Validate that API latency returns to baseline after the restart without manual intervention

recommendations.title: Scale things horizontally and make clients retry with idempotent, ETag-guarded writes
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 2ee196bc306c (risk LOW 2.4/10), API success fell to 50% during injection, TTR 6 s. Things actors are cluster-sharded, so a second instance lets Pekko re-home shards instead of waiting for the crashed JVM to restart. On the client side, every Thing write in Ditto is a PUT with `If-Match`/ETag support, so retries are safe and cheap.
steps: Run `things` with `deploy.replicas: 2` (compose) or `replicas: 2` (k8s); keep the Pekko seed-node list stable.
Set a sensible `pekko.cluster.sharding.rebalance-interval` / `passivation` so shards move within a few seconds of a node loss.
In client SDKs, wrap PUT/PATCH with 3 retries + exponential backoff on 5xx/connection errors and send `If-Match: <etag>` to make the retry idempotent; treat 412 as 'already applied'.
Keep POST-created things (server-generated ids) behind a client-side idempotency key or prefer PUT with a client-chosen thingId.
verify: Kill one things instance: API success stays > 90% and the cluster view shows the shard regions rebalanced.
A retried PUT with a stale `If-Match` returns 412 rather than overwriting newer state.

recommendations.title: Run MongoDB as a replica set so the Ditto driver can fail over
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7c359ebe3c68 (risk LOW 0.4/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 9 s. MongoDB is the sole datastore for policies, things, things-search and connectivity. A single standalone mongod turns any Mongo hiccup into a full-platform outage; a replica set lets the Java driver elect a new primary and keep serving within seconds.
steps: Start mongod with `--replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all` (compose `command:`) and run `rs.initiate()` once via an init container or `docker exec`.
Add two more members (or one member plus an arbiter for the lab) on separate volumes.
Point the Ditto services at the set: `MONGO_DB_URI=mongodb://mongodb-0:27017,mongodb-1:27017,mongodb-2:27017/ditto?replicaSet=rs0&w=majority`.
Set `retryWrites=true&retryReads=true` on the URI so transient primary step-downs are retried by the driver.
verify: `docker exec mongodb mongosh --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.stateStr)'` shows one PRIMARY and ≥1 SECONDARY.
Re-run the same chaos experiment against the primary only; API success rate during injection should stay above the abort threshold and TTR should drop below 15 s.

recommendations.title: Add a MongoDB healthcheck and an autoheal sidecar to the compose stack
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7c359ebe3c68 (risk LOW 0.4/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 9 s. Docker's `restart: always` only reacts to a process exit; a container that is running but marked `unhealthy` is never restarted. Without a healthcheck on mongodb nothing even notices a wedged database, and dependents that lost their connection just sit there.
steps: Add to the mongodb service: `healthcheck: {test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"], interval: 10s, timeout: 5s, retries: 3, start_period: 20s}`.
Add an `autoheal` service: `image: willfarrell/autoheal`, `environment: [AUTOHEAL_CONTAINER_LABEL=all]`, mount `/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro`, `restart: always`.
Label the Ditto services with `autoheal=true` (or keep `AUTOHEAL_CONTAINER_LABEL=all`) so an `unhealthy` state triggers a restart.
verify: `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' mongodb` reports `healthy` at steady state.
Pause mongodb for 60 s: autoheal logs show a restart of the unhealthy dependents within ~30 s of them flipping to unhealthy.

recommendations.title: Tune Ditto's MongoDB client timeouts and connection pool
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7c359ebe3c68 (risk LOW 0.4/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 9 s. With default driver settings a stalled Mongo socket can hold a request thread for tens of seconds, which inflates p95 and keeps the health endpoints green while users see timeouts. Explicit, short timeouts turn a hang into a fast, retryable error.
steps: Set connection/read timeouts on the Ditto services; Ditto reads `MONGO_DB_*` environment variables (e.g. `MONGO_DB_CONNECTION_POOL_SIZE`, `MONGO_DB_READ_PREFERENCE`, `MONGO_DB_QUERY_TIMEOUT`) — verify exact names against `ditto-mongo.conf` in the Ditto source and the operating docs before applying.
Alternatively encode them in the URI: `?connectTimeoutMS=3000&socketTimeoutMS=10000&serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000&maxPoolSize=100`.
Keep `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` well below the nginx `proxy_read_timeout` so the edge sees a clean 5xx instead of a hung connection.
verify: During a `network_delay` experiment on mongodb the p95 should plateau near the configured timeout instead of growing unbounded.
`docker logs things | grep -i 'MongoTimeout'` shows fast failures rather than minute-long waits.

recommendations.title: Set explicit timeouts end to end and add a circuit breaker at the API edge
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7c359ebe3c68 (risk LOW 0.4/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 9 s. Latency injected into one hop propagated to the user as long hangs instead of fast failures. Without aligned timeouts each layer waits for the slowest one beneath it, request threads pile up, and the whole API degrades rather than the one slow path.
steps: nginx: `proxy_connect_timeout 2s; proxy_send_timeout 10s; proxy_read_timeout 30s;` and `proxy_next_upstream timeout`.

Ditto gateway: lower the request timeout (`ditto.gateway.http.request-timeout` / `GATEWAY_HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, default 60 s) to ~15 s; have clients send the `timeout` query parameter on commands (e.g. `?timeout=10s`) so Ditto fails fast instead of hanging.
Add a circuit breaker in front of the gateway (nginx `max_fails`/`fail_timeout`, or Envoy outlier detection) so a degraded backend sheds load for a few seconds instead of queuing.
Align Mongo driver `socketTimeoutMS` below the gateway timeout so the failure surfaces as a clean error with a cause.
verify: Replay `network_delay` with the same latency: p95 is capped near the smallest configured timeout and the error budget burn is measurable rather than a hang.
No request in the probe log exceeds the nginx `proxy_read_timeout`.

recommendations.title: Baseline observability: SLO alert rules and chaos annotations in Grafana
recommendations.rationale: In experiment 7c359ebe3c68 (risk LOW 0.4/10), API success fell to 100% during injection, TTR 9 s. Whatever the specific fault, the first production improvement is knowing within a minute that users are affected. Alert on what the user sees (probe success, error rate, p95), not only on container liveness.
steps: Prometheus rules: `probe_success == 0 for 1m` (blackbox on `/api/2/things` through nginx), API error-rate SLO burn (`sum(rate(requests{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests[5m])) > 0.02`), and `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) > 1s for 5m`.
Add a Grafana annotation (HTTP API `POST /api/annotations`, tag `chaos`) at the start and end of each Faultline experiment so latency spikes are attributable.
Dashboard the Docker health state per container (`container_health_status` via cAdvisor or a tiny exporter) next to the API SLIs.
verify: During the next experiment an alert fires within 60 s of the first API error and the Grafana graph shows the chaos window.

recommendations.title: Make readiness reflect subsystem health, and alert on /status/health
recommendations.rationale: In experiment fd1b18f67001 (risk HIGH 5.8/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 30 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. The service kept answering `/ready` with 200 while the API was failing, so no orchestrator or alert could react. Ditto issue #1865 describes exactly this: the Pekko cluster was healthy but the persistence subsystem was not, and PR #1867 added a `subsystem-health` check under `management.health-checks.liveness-checks`.
steps: Upgrade to a Ditto release containing PR #1867 (3.6+) and confirm `management.health-checks.liveness-checks.subsystem-health` is enabled.

Verify whether the equivalent subsystem check is wired into the readiness checks for your version; if not, add it (or treat `/status/health` as the readiness probe in compose/k8s instead of `/ready`).
Point the compose `healthcheck` of each Ditto service at `http://localhost:8558/status/health` (requires devops credentials or `DEVOPS_SECURED=false` in the lab) and fail on any `DOWN` component.
Add a Prometheus alert on `probe_success{job="ditto-health"} == 0` and on the API error-rate SLO, not only on `/alive`.
verify: Stop mongodb: within one healthcheck interval the Ditto services report `unhealthy` in `docker ps` and `/status/health` shows the persistence component `DOWN`.
The `health_check_masked_failure` finding no longer appears when the experiment is replayed.

recommendations.title: Scale things horizontally and make clients retry with idempotent, ETag-guarded writes
recommendations.rationale: In experiment fd1b18f67001 (risk HIGH 5.8/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 30 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. Things actors are cluster-sharded, so a second instance lets Pekko re-home shards instead of waiting for the crashed JVM to restart. On the client side, every Thing write in Ditto is a PUT with `If-Match`/ETag support, so retries are safe and cheap.
steps: Run `things` with `deploy.replicas: 2` (compose) or `replicas: 2` (k8s); keep the Pekko seed-node list stable.
Set a sensible `pekko.cluster.sharding.rebalance-interval` / `passivation` so shards move within a few seconds of a node loss.
In client SDKs, wrap PUT/PATCH with 3 retries + exponential backoff on 5xx/connection errors and send `If-Match: <etag>` to make the retry idempotent; treat 412 as 'already applied'.
Keep POST-created things (server-generated ids) behind a client-side idempotency key or prefer PUT with a client-chosen thingId.
verify: Kill one things instance: API success stays > 90% and the cluster view shows the shard regions rebalanced.
A retried PUT with a stale `If-Match` returns 412 rather than overwriting newer state.

weaknesses.why_it_matters: Traffic can reach grafana without passing the proxy, so whatever the proxy does for the rest of the stack -- auth, timeouts, rate limiting -- does not protect this path.
weaknesses.label: [predicted, unconfirmed]

weaknesses.title: nginx has no CPU limit
weaknesses.evidence: compose service `nginx`: no `deploy.resources.limits.cpus` (it does set memory limit `32m`). Nothing bounds its share of the host, so a CPU spike inside it degrades every other container on the same machine.

suggested_experiment.reason: load nginx and watch whether the cgroup contains it

weaknesses.why_it_matters: nginx can take the host down with it. With that limit unset nothing bounds nginx's share of the machine, so a spike inside it starves every other container instead of being throttled inside its own cgroup.
weaknesses.label: [predicted, unconfirmed]

weaknesses.title: prometheus publishes a port of its own besides the nginx ingress
weaknesses.evidence: compose service `prometheus`: `ports: ['127.0.0.1:9090:9090']` while `nginx` is the declared entrypoint -- all bound to 127.0.0.1, so the sandbox boundary itself holds. Traffic can reach `prometheus` without passing the proxy, so proxy-level protections do not apply to it. This service is tagged outside the system under test, so the extra surface is deliberate rather than an oversight.
